paragraphs: The paper tackles estimation of a sparse inverse covariance matrix for a multivariate normal distribution. The assumption of sparsity means that many entries of the desired matrix are zero. A standard approach combines a log-determinant objective with an l1 penalty that encourages this structure. At large scales, however, memory requirements prevent many existing algorithms from handling the problem.

The proposed method uses block-coordinate descent: it works on portions of the matrix rather than treating every entry as one simultaneous update. Within this process, quadratic approximations provide simpler local problems to solve. This changes how the established estimation objective is approached, making the organization of the computation central to addressing large instances.

Experiments on synthetic data and real gene expression data show better performance than the state-of-the-art methods considered, especially on large problems. The contribution is therefore a computational approach to sparse inverse covariance estimation whose reported advantages become particularly relevant when the size of the matrix makes existing methods difficult to use.
neurips-2014-a-block-coordinate-descent-.tldr: A block-coordinate descent method improves large-scale sparse inverse covariance estimation by updating matrix blocks through quadratic approximations.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference makes Bayesian computation manageable on massive datasets by using noisy optimization updates. This paper interprets those updates as an approximate form of parallel coordinate ascent. From that perspective, the task is to move toward the coordinate optimum that batch variational Bayes would provide, while balancing the bias and variance of noisy information.

The authors turn this balancing act into an inference problem. A model uses a sequence of noisy realizations to estimate where the next batch optimum lies. Variational parameters are then updated through Bayes rule, replacing a manually designed optimization schedule with a probabilistic account of the update process.

With a Kalman filter as the model, the framework can recover both original SVI and versions with adaptive steps. It can also express additional assumptions, including heavy-tailed noise. Using such modeling choices, the proposed algorithm outperforms the original schedule and a state-of-the-art adaptive SVI method in two domains. These results support filtering as a useful way to design and adapt variational updates.
neurips-2014-a-filtering-approach-to-sto.tldr: Treating noisy variational updates as a filtering problem yields Bayesian update rules that recover and extend stochastic variational inference.

paragraphs: This paper addresses retrieval in datasets containing multiple kinds of information. Its central goal is to learn abstract features that carry semantic meaning across those modalities, then use those features to support search. A cross-modal query asks the system to retrieve information across modality boundaries, making the relationship between different representations central to the task.

The proposed procedure has three connected parts. A nonparametric Bayesian latent feature framework learns the underlying representation. A probabilistic retrieval model then uses that representation to support cross-modal queries. An additional model incorporates relevance feedback, extending the procedure beyond its initial retrieval stage. Together, these components connect representation learning, retrieval, and feedback within a probabilistic framework.

The authors evaluate the procedure on PASCAL-Sentence and SUN-Attribute. The experiments demonstrate its effectiveness compared with state-of-the-art algorithms for learning binary codes. The stated contribution is a complete retrieval procedure built around semantically meaningful latent features, with empirical support on two multimodal datasets for using that representation in cross-modal search.
neurips-2014-a-probabilistic-framework-f.tldr: A Bayesian latent feature framework combines multimodal representation learning, cross-modal retrieval, and relevance feedback.

paragraphs: The paper studies principal component estimation for tensors under a model consisting of one rank-one signal plus noise. It separates two questions: whether the signal can be estimated at all, and whether particular computationally efficient algorithms can estimate it. This distinction exposes a gap between information available in the data and information accessible through the analyzed methods.

With unrestricted computation, the authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions for estimation. In particular, estimation is possible when the signal-to-noise ratio exceeds C times the square root of k log k, where k is tensor order; for fixed order, this ratio can remain bounded as dimensions grow. The polynomial-time methods analyzed, based on unfolding, power iteration, and message passing, instead require the ratio to grow with dimension.

The authors suggest that this gap may reflect a fundamental computational limitation, without establishing that conclusion for every efficient estimator. They also propose an unfolding-and-power-iteration hybrid that substantially improves on baselines at moderate dimensions, and characterize how much side information enables iterative methods to reach a good estimate.
neurips-2014-a-statistical-model-for-ten.tldr: A rank-one tensor model reveals a gap between statistical recoverability and the signal strength required by several efficient estimation algorithms.

paragraphs: Persistent activity occurs when cortical neurons continue firing after the stimulus that triggered them has disappeared. It is widely regarded as a possible basis for retaining a memory trace. Conventional accounts treat this activity as an attractor of network dynamics, but then need to explain how the persistent state ends at an appropriate time.

The paper explores a different account: stimulus information occupies a marginally unstable network state that decays slowly. Such a state can sustain firing for a prolonged period while still eventually disappearing. The proposed mechanism uses short-term synaptic plasticity, specifically depression and facilitation, which have opposing effects on the retention of neuronal responses.

The authors find that an appropriate combination of these two effects can produce persistent activity with different lifetimes. The activity also fades naturally without an external drive to terminate it. This provides a proposed mechanism that links temporary information retention and its eventual disappearance, and motivates discussion of how neural systems might represent information through activity that lasts for a controllable duration.
neurips-2014-a-synaptical-story-of-persi.tldr: Combining short-term synaptic facilitation and depression can produce persistent neural activity with variable lifetimes that ends naturally.

paragraphs: Maximum inner product search seeks items with the largest inner product with a query, without requiring vectors to be normalized. The paper addresses the difficulty of building fast hashing schemes for this similarity measure. It presents what the authors describe as the first provably sublinear-time hashing algorithm for approximate maximum inner product search.

The central change is to allow asymmetric hashing. Independent transformations convert the inner product search problem into approximate near-neighbor search in a classical setting. This expands the existing locality-sensitive hashing framework and makes it possible to construct an explicit scheme with a provable speed guarantee. The approximation concerns the search result; the sublinear guarantee concerns how search time scales.

The authors also report a simple implementation and evaluate it for collaborative-filtering recommendations on Netflix and Movielens datasets. Their scheme provides significant computational savings over sign random projection and L2 hashing based on p-stable distributions. The results connect the transformation-based argument to a practical retrieval task where inner products determine which items should be recommended.
neurips-2014-asymmetric-lsh-alsh-for-sub.tldr: Asymmetric transformations enable provably sublinear approximate maximum inner product search through locality-sensitive hashing.

paragraphs: Many partitioning problems describe relationships among several objects at once, rather than only pairs. The paper studies this setting through random uniform hypergraphs, where every hyperedge involves the same number m of objects. Its aim is to give theoretical support for spectral partitioning when the input contains these multi-way affinities.

The authors develop a planted partition model, also described as a stochastic blockmodel, using higher-order tensors. This supplies a probabilistic setting with an underlying partition against which an algorithm can be analyzed. They then present a suitable spectral method and investigate its behavior as sample size becomes large.

The analysis establishes consistency for larger values of m and finds that convergence improves as m increases within the studied setting. Thus, the result gives theoretical evidence that higher-order affinities can help partition recovery. The significance is tied to the random model and its large-sample analysis: the paper supplies a reason that relationships involving more objects can improve spectral partitioning under this formulation.
neurips-2014-consistency-of-spectral-par.tldr: A planted-partition analysis establishes spectral consistency for uniform hypergraphs and faster convergence with increasing affinity order in the studied setting.

paragraphs: Recursive neural networks can process structured language input, using parse trees to model how meanings combine. Although a tree creates depth through its structure, the authors argue that this does not provide the same hierarchical representation capacity as multiple layers in conventional deep networks. The paper addresses that distinction between structural depth and representation depth.

The proposed architecture stacks several recursive layers. This allows the model to build multiple levels of representation while retaining its ability to operate on structured input. The authors evaluate the architecture on fine-grained sentiment classification and compare it with associated shallow models having the same number of parameters, making depth a meaningful part of the comparison.

The deep models outperform those shallow counterparts and earlier sentiment baselines, including a multiplicative recursive network variant and paragraph vectors, achieving the reported state of the art. Exploratory analyses suggest that different layers capture different aspects of language composition. These findings support stacked recursive processing as a useful way to improve sentiment representations beyond merely increasing parameter count.
neurips-2014-deep-recursive-neural-netwo.tldr: Stacking recursive neural layers improves fine-grained sentiment classification over equally sized shallow counterparts and the reported earlier baselines.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer probabilistic models of functions, including uncertainty estimates and principled hyperparameter tuning. They are useful for regression and nonlinear dimensionality reduction, but applying them to large datasets raises computational challenges. This paper develops distributed inference for sparse Gaussian process regression and latent variable models.

The method reparameterizes variational inference by exploiting how data decouple when conditioned on inducing points. This lets the authors reformulate the evidence lower bound, the objective used for approximate inference, in a Map-Reduce setting. The resulting computation can be distributed across nodes, and the authors report good scaling with both data volume and computational resources while maintaining balanced workloads.

Experiments show that Gaussian process performance improves as more data are used, both for regression on two million flight records and for latent variable modeling on MNIST. The models also outperform many common approaches used for big data in the reported results. The contribution connects a reformulation of the inference objective to evidence that larger datasets can improve these probabilistic models.
neurips-2014-distributed-variational-inf.tldr: A variational reparameterization enables distributed sparse Gaussian process inference with balanced workloads and improved performance as data increase.

paragraphs: Fisher vector coding represents image features through gradients of a generative model. Common implementations use Gaussian mixtures, which work well with relatively low-dimensional local features. The paper argues that a comparable number of mixture components does not adequately model higher-dimensional features, while simply adding many more Gaussians becomes computationally impractical.

The proposed model draws each local feature from a Gaussian whose mean is itself sampled from a subspace. Under an approximation, learning and inference become a sparse coding problem that standard methods can solve. The authors then derive a Fisher vector representation from this model's gradients, calling the resulting approach sparse coding based Fisher vector coding.

For image classification, the method uses deep convolutional network descriptors as high-dimensional local features. Experiments show significant improvements over traditional Gaussian-mixture Fisher vectors and report state-of-the-art performance in generic object recognition, indoor scene classification, and fine-grained classification. The approach addresses the modeling challenge by changing how feature variation is represented, with evidence of benefits across the tested classification settings.
neurips-2014-encoding-high-dimensional-l.tldr: A sparse coding generative model produces Fisher vectors better suited to high-dimensional local image features.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Bayesian approach to training deterministic multilayer neural networks. It approximates the posterior distribution of weights with a factorized, mean-field distribution in an online setting. Using expectation propagation and the central limit theorem, the authors derive analytical approximations to posterior updates and to estimates of network weights and outputs.

The resulting expectation backpropagation algorithm resembles ordinary backpropagation in form and efficiency. Its training is parameter-free once the prior and network architecture are specified. It also permits discrete weights, which the authors identify as useful for precision-limited hardware with potential speed and energy-efficiency advantages. The prior and architecture remain part of the setup.

On eight binary text classification tasks, expectation backpropagation outperforms standard backpropagation with the optimal constant learning rate and previously reported state-of-the-art results. Networks with binary weights usually perform better than those with continuous weights when outputs are averaged using the inferred posterior. That qualification matters: the reported binary-weight advantage concerns posterior-averaged predictions, rather than an unconditional advantage of binary weights.
neurips-2014-expectation-backpropagation.tldr: Expectation backpropagation derives efficient Bayesian training updates for continuous or discrete network weights, given a prior and architecture.

paragraphs: Local differential privacy protects personal information even from the analyst receiving released data. The paper studies how much statistical usefulness can be retained under this protection when both providers and analysts want useful inferences. It frames the tradeoff using information-theoretic utility functions and asks which privatization mechanisms maximize those utilities.

The authors introduce staircase mechanisms and prove that this family contains an optimal mechanism. For every information-theoretic utility function studied in the paper, utility maximization can be expressed as a linear program whose solution selects an optimal staircase mechanism. This gives a concrete optimization formulation, although the number of variables grows exponentially with data size and can make computation expensive.

The paper also identifies simpler choices. Within the studied setting, the binary mechanism is universally optimal in the high-privacy regime, while randomized response is universally optimal in the low-privacy regime. Both approximate the intermediate regime well. These results make the abstract privacy-utility tradeoff more actionable by connecting exact optimality to a structured family and practical choices to privacy strength.
neurips-2014-extremal-mechanisms-for-loc.tldr: Staircase mechanisms characterize optimal local privacy-utility tradeoffs, with simple optimal choices in the high- and low-privacy regimes studied.

paragraphs: Learning algorithms often face restrictions on how they access or retain training information. They may have little memory, process examples sequentially, communicate only limited information between machines, or observe only part of each example. The paper asks how such restrictions can affect performance independently of the particular interpretation of the learning task.

Its central question concerns fundamental limits rather than the shortcomings of a chosen implementation. Are there problems where every algorithm with a small memory budget, a bounded number of usable bits per example, or specified communication restrictions performs worse than an unrestricted algorithm? Establishing this would show that better algorithm design alone cannot always remove the cost of restricted information access.

The authors give a single set of results that answers these questions positively in several settings. The conclusion is existential: there are learning problems where the constraints impose an unavoidable disadvantage. By connecting multiple settings through common results, the paper treats memory, communication, and data-access restrictions as related sources of statistical difficulty.
neurips-2014-fundamental-limits-of-onlin.tldr: A unified set of results shows that memory, communication, and information-access restrictions can impose unavoidable learning disadvantages.

paragraphs: Learning control policies becomes difficult when a system has large continuous spaces and complex dynamics. The paper proposes a policy search method that learns local linear descriptions of those dynamics and repeatedly refits them. These models help optimize distributions over trajectories, providing guidance for learning policies through guided policy search.

The dynamics models vary over time and describe local behavior, avoiding the need to learn one global model of the whole system. That choice matters when dynamics are nonsmooth or discontinuous. The optimized trajectory distributions can guide policies with arbitrary parameterizations, including neural networks, so the local modeling strategy does not require the final policy to share its linear form.

The authors show that the hybrid approach needs many fewer samples than model-free methods and can handle complex, nonsmooth dynamics. Experiments demonstrate neural network policies performing simulated robotic manipulation tasks with partial observation, numerous contact discontinuities, and underactuation. These findings support local model fitting as a way to guide learning in the challenging control settings tested.
neurips-2014-learning-neural-network-pol.tldr: Repeatedly fitted local dynamics models guide neural policy learning with fewer samples in simulated manipulation tasks involving complex dynamics.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a common framework for supervised learning and semi-supervised learning, where labeled and unlabeled data are used together. Its starting point is to rewrite the learning problem as a regularized Fredholm integral equation. This gives a mathematical formulation that fits within kernel methods while changing how the learning problem is represented.

The same approach can be understood as constructing new kernels that depend on the data. The authors call these Fredholm kernels. This interpretation connects the integral-equation formulation to the kernel framework, making the construction of a data-dependent kernel the bridge between the mathematical reformulation and its use for learning.

For semi-supervised learning, the authors examine a condition they call the noise assumption. They provide both theoretical and experimental evidence that Fredholm kernels can use unlabeled data effectively under that assumption. They also report very competitive performance in the standard semi-supervised setting. The findings therefore link the value of unlabeled data to a stated assumption and support the proposed formulation with both analysis and experiments.
neurips-2014-learning-with-fredholm-kern.tldr: Fredholm kernels recast learning through regularized integral equations and can exploit unlabeled data under the paper's noise assumption.

paragraphs: Boosted decision trees are effective for fast object detection, but many use splits based on one feature at a time. When features are strongly correlated, those splits may fit the structure of the data poorly. Splits that combine several features can help, but the paper identifies their computational expense as a practical obstacle.

The authors instead transform the features to remove correlations within local neighborhoods. This produces an overcomplete, locally decorrelated representation designed to work well with single-feature tree splits. The central idea is to make the representation more compatible with inexpensive decision rules, moving the treatment of local feature relationships into the feature transform.

In the reported comparisons, ordinary orthogonal trees using the transformed representation outperform oblique trees trained on the original features at a fraction of the computational cost. On the Caltech Pedestrian Dataset, the method reduces false positives nearly tenfold relative to the previous state of the art. These findings demonstrate a substantial detection improvement from changing the representation while retaining simple tree splits.
neurips-2014-local-decorrelation-for-imp.tldr: Locally decorrelating features makes simple decision trees more effective for pedestrian detection, with nearly tenfold fewer false positives in the reported benchmark.

paragraphs: Computing a massive graph's leading eigenvalues and eigenvectors is important in machine learning, but common solvers can converge slowly when many components are needed. MSEIGS approaches this computation at multiple scales. It first partitions the graph into smaller clusters whose spectral decompositions can be computed efficiently and independently.

The authors show theoretically and empirically that, when clustering is appropriate, the cluster subspaces overlap substantially with the original graph's dominant subspace. Cluster eigenvectors therefore provide useful starting points for a block Lanczos algorithm on the full graph. Hierarchical clustering further accelerates computation, and an early stopping strategy produces useful approximations.

The method improves convergence speed and approximation quality over widely used solvers in the reported comparisons, and supports shared-memory parallelism. On a graph exceeding 82 million nodes and 3.6 billion edges, it approximates the top 50 eigenvectors in under three hours on one core, versus over six hours for randomized SVD at similar quality. With 16 cores, its time falls below 40 minutes.
neurips-2014-multi-scale-spectral-decomp.tldr: MSEIGS uses cluster-level spectral decompositions to initialize and accelerate leading-eigenvector computation on massive graphs.

paragraphs: Submodular functions arise in discrete problems across machine learning, signal processing, and computer vision. Minimizing them can nevertheless be algorithmically difficult. This paper studies the case where the objective decomposes into a sum of simpler submodular functions, a structure used by an existing algorithm that is easy to apply and can run in parallel.

That algorithm had already shown strong empirical performance, but lacked a theoretical convergence analysis. The authors establish linear convergence, meaning that progress follows a geometric rate rather than merely a fixed reduction in error per iteration. They also provide both upper and lower bounds on the convergence rate, giving a more informative characterization than eventual convergence alone.

The proof combines the geometry of submodular polyhedra with results from spectral graph theory. Its contribution is to explain the behavior of an existing practical method through mathematical analysis. By bounding its convergence rate in the decomposable setting, the paper supplies theoretical support for an algorithm whose appeal had previously rested on empirical results.
neurips-2014-on-the-convergence-rate-of-.tldr: The paper proves linear convergence and bounds its rate for an existing parallelizable algorithm for decomposable submodular minimization.

paragraphs: The paper studies Hamiltonian Monte Carlo through a geometric formulation. It uses the Jacobi metric, a construction from mathematical physics, to describe each HMC step as a geodesic on a Riemannian manifold. A geodesic is the geometric path associated with the metric, so this viewpoint turns the sampler's movement into a question about the shape of its underlying space.

The authors calculate sectional curvature for this HMC manifold. Their calculation shows positive curvature in cases including sampling from a high-dimensional multivariate Gaussian. The curvature result therefore applies to identified sampling settings and provides a geometric property that can be brought into the theoretical analysis of the chain.

They then show that positive curvature can support proofs of concentration results for HMC Markov chains. The contribution is a connection between the geometry of HMC trajectories and probabilistic guarantees about the resulting chain. This makes the Jacobi-metric viewpoint useful beyond a reinterpretation of the algorithm: its curvature supplies a tool for proving theoretical behavior in applicable cases.
neurips-2014-positive-curvature-and-hami.tldr: A Jacobi-metric formulation connects positive curvature in certain HMC settings to theoretical concentration results.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the perception that kernel methods cannot scale to large nonlinear learning problems. It builds on the fact that many kernel methods have convex optimization formulations. The proposed algorithm performs descent using functional gradients estimated through two sources of randomness: sampled training points and random features associated with the kernel.

Both stochastic approximations are unbiased. Their combination gives a noisy update without requiring commitment to a fixed number of random features in advance. In a streaming setting, the flexibility of the function class can grow as more data arrive. The authors prove convergence to the optimal function in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space at rate O(1/t), alongside a generalization bound of O(1/sqrt(t)).

Experiments report competitive performance against neural networks on large datasets involving energy materials, handwritten digits, and photographs represented with convolutional features. These findings support the claim that this optimization strategy can bring kernel methods into large-data regimes commonly associated with neural networks. The contribution combines scalable updates, an expandable representation, and stated theoretical guarantees.
neurips-2014-scalable-kernel-methods-via.tldr: Randomizing over both training points and kernel features yields scalable kernel learning with convergence guarantees and an expandable representation.

paragraphs: In some regression problems, nonzero coefficients occur in groups or regions rather than independently. The paper calls this region sparsity. Standard sparse approaches such as lasso and automatic relevance determination do not exploit this dependence in their prior modeling. The authors seek a model that captures both clustered nonzero weights and smooth variation.

Their hierarchical extension of relevance determination uses a transformed Gaussian process to connect the prior variances of regression weights. They combine it with a structured model for the prior variances of Fourier coefficients, suppressing unnecessary high frequencies. Together, these choices encourage region sparsity in two bases and provide a model for smooth weight vectors and tensors in linear regression.

The authors develop efficient approximate inference procedures and evaluate the model on simulated data and real brain imaging datasets. They report substantial improvements over comparable approaches, including group lasso and smooth RVM. These results support explicitly representing dependence among relevant coefficients when the desired regression structure includes both spatial grouping and smoothness.
neurips-2014-sparse-bayesian-structure-l.tldr: Dependent relevance determination models clustered, smooth regression weights through linked prior variances in the original and Fourier representations.

paragraphs: Supervised topic models connect two kinds of information: the hidden topics within documents and a response associated with each document. Learning these models requires recovering parameters that describe that joint structure. The paper introduces Spectral-sLDA, a spectral decomposition algorithm for supervised latent Dirichlet allocation, providing an alternative to inference based on variational approximation or Monte Carlo sampling.

The authors establish correctness and computational efficiency for the algorithm. They also prove a sample complexity bound, which addresses the amount of data needed for parameter recovery. From this analysis, they derive a sufficient condition for identifiability: a condition under which the model's parameters can be distinguished. Sufficiency means that satisfying the condition provides a guarantee, without claiming it is the only possible route to identification.

Experiments across synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical analysis and demonstrate practical effectiveness. The contribution combines a parameter-recovery algorithm with guarantees about recovery and identifiability, connecting an alternative computational method to evidence that it works in the evaluated document-modeling settings.
neurips-2014-spectral-methods-for-superv.tldr: Spectral-sLDA recovers supervised topic-model parameters with correctness and sample-complexity guarantees, supported by synthetic and real-data experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies community recovery in large sparse networks with a finite number of disjoint clusters. Connections are denser within communities than between them, but both densities vanish as the graph grows. This makes recovery increasingly noisy while the adjacency matrix becomes difficult to store. The authors consider a stream in which its columns arrive sequentially.

They develop two algorithms with asymptotically accurate cluster recovery. The offline version retains node assignments and uses memory proportional to network size. The online version can classify a node when its column arrives and then discard that information, requiring memory that grows sublinearly. The distinction directly links the retained output information to the memory requirement.

To construct these methods, the authors first study clustering when only a small fraction of adjacency-matrix columns is available. They develop a spectral algorithm for that partial-information problem, which also has independent interest. The overall result shows how limited observations and sequential access can support asymptotically accurate recovery under the paper's sparse, non-overlapping community setting.
neurips-2014-streaming-memory-limited-al.tldr: Two streaming algorithms recover communities asymptotically accurately in the studied sparse networks, with linear or sublinear memory depending on retained assignments.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms, including gradient descent with or without weight decay, predict using linear combinations of previously observed instances. The paper constructs random example sets where the target linear predictor is easy to learn, yet every algorithm in this family is drastically suboptimal. The result separates an easy learning target from restrictions imposed by a particular algorithmic form.

The lower bound continues to hold when the algorithms can use an arbitrary kernel. While such a result was already known for square loss, the authors develop techniques that extend it to losses meeting minimal requirements, including logistic and hinge loss. They also show that methods regularized by squared Euclidean distance can be confused by random features.

The paper closes with related questions about feed-forward neural networks. It conjectures that the hardness results extend to any training method based on squared Euclidean distance regularization, including backpropagation with weight decay. This extension remains a conjecture in the supplied account; the established results concern the analyzed algorithm family and constructed learning problems.
neurips-2014-the-limits-of-squared-eucli.tldr: Constructed learning problems expose severe limitations of predictors built from past instances, with related neural-network extensions posed as conjectures.

paragraphs: Recognizing an action in video requires information about both appearance and movement. A still frame provides spatial information, while changes between frames provide temporal information. This paper develops a two-stream convolutional network architecture with separate spatial and temporal networks to capture these complementary sources within a learned approach to action recognition.

The temporal network is trained on dense optical flow across multiple frames. The authors show that this motion input supports very good performance despite limited training data. They also apply multi-task learning across two action classification datasets, increasing the amount of training data available and improving performance on both datasets.

The architecture is trained and evaluated on UCF-101 and HMDB-51, where it is competitive with the state of the art and substantially exceeds earlier deep-network approaches to video classification. The findings support an architecture that explicitly represents appearance and motion, while showing that motion-focused learning and training across datasets can help address the limited-data setting considered.
neurips-2014-two-stream-convolutional-ne.tldr: Separate appearance and motion ConvNets achieve competitive video action recognition, with multi-task training improving results on both evaluated datasets.
